title: Island Whiskies of Scotland | Craft Beer School
desc: A tour of Scotland's island whiskies beyond Islay, from Orkney to Skye, Mull, Jura and Arran, with the styles each island is known for.
teaser: Skye, Orkney, Jura, Mull, Arran and Lewis all make whisky. They share an ocean, not a style.
standfirst: Scotland's island malts are often talked about as one region. Officially they are not one at all. Here is how the islands fit into the Scotch rules and what each one tends to put in the glass.
sections: The Islands are not an official region

The Scotch Whisky Regulations protect five regional names: Highland, Lowland, Speyside, Campbeltown and Islay. Islay is an island with its own region. The other islands are legally part of the Highland region.

Retailers and writers still group them as Island whiskies because the style differs from mainland Highland malts and a sixth label is handy. That is fine for shopping. Just do not expect one shared house style, the way people talk about Speyside.

Orkney lies off the north coast of mainland Scotland. Its two distilleries make malts known for honey, heather and a soft, aromatic smoke.

That smoke is the part worth understanding. Peat is partly decomposed plant matter. Orkney peat formed largely from heather, sedge and moss with few trees, because the islands are windswept. Islay peat contains more seaweed and coastal plant material. Different plants give different phenolic compounds when the peat is burnt to dry the malt, so Orkney smoke tends to read floral and earthy rather than medicinal.

The Isle of Skye on the west coast is home to a famous peated malt known for black pepper, sea spray and a big, warming smoke. A second distillery opened on the island more recently.

The peppery note is the classic Skye signature. On the palate it builds after you swallow, a prickle at the back of the tongue that is separate from the alcohol heat. Learning to tell that pepper from simple burn is a good exercise for any taster. Our guide to tasting past the alcohol burn helps.
Mull, Jura, Arran and the rest

The Isle of Mull has one distillery making both unpeated and peated malts. Jura, next to Islay, makes mostly lightly peated or unpeated whisky with a softer, fruitier profile than its famous neighbour. Arran, in the Firth of Clyde, makes a clean, fruity unpeated malt and a peated one too.

Newer distilleries have opened on islands including Lewis and Harris in the Outer Hebrides and Raasay off Skye. Because they are young, their bottlings are often three to eight years old. Expect them to taste of the spirit and the cask more than of any island tradition.
What the islands really have in common

The honest answer is that the islands share remoteness more than flavour. That remoteness affects how they work. Barley, casks and fuel arrive by ferry. Spent grain and finished spirit leave the same way. Many island distilleries send their spirit to the mainland to mature in large warehouses, while others mature at least part of it on the island.

Remote and small often means a single distillery shapes an entire island's reputation. One cask policy or one peat level can define how a whole island is described. When you taste, credit the distillery's choices, not the postcode.
Reading an island label before you buy

Because the islands sit inside the Highland region, an island malt may say Highland single malt on the label, or simply name the island. Neither tells you the peat level. Look for words such as peated, smoky or unpeated. Then look for the producer's own description of the cask.

The cask line matters as much as the island. A Skye malt finished in sherry casks and the same spirit from refill ex-bourbon casks are very different drinks. Check the ABV too. Many island bottlings sit at 40 to 46% ABV. Above about 46% ABV and without chill filtration, a whisky often feels fuller and oilier, which can make a coastal malt taste more like itself.

Age statements help when you compare within one island. A 10 year old and an 18 year old from the same distillery show how the cask slowly rounds off smoke and pepper over time. Our guide to comparing age statements side by side sets that tasting out.

Pour about 25 ml of each into tulip glasses. Start with the unpeated or lightly peated malts, then move to the smoky ones. Smoke lingers on the palate and will mask anything delicate you taste after it.

If your room is warm, as most Indian rooms are for much of the year, pour just before you nose. Use a cover on the glass between sniffs so the top notes do not escape. Add water drop by drop. Keep a jug of water for drinking too, pace the tasting and never drink and drive.

Telling heather smoke from coastal smoke takes real practice. Most people can tell smoky from not smoky on day one. Naming the kind of smoke is where structured nosing practice pays off.
Pick two islands and compare their smoke

Your first step: taste one Orkney malt beside one Skye malt. Both are smoky. Write one line on the smoke in each, in your own words. If one says bonfire and heather and the other says pepper and sea, you have just found the island difference that a map cannot show you.
faqs: Is Islands an official Scotch whisky region?
No. The islands other than Islay are legally part of the Highland region. Island is an informal grouping used by retailers and writers.
Islay aside, whisky is made on Orkney, Skye, Mull, Jura, Arran, Raasay and Lewis and Harris, among others.
No. Many island distilleries make unpeated malts alongside peated ones. The type of smoke varies by island.
